summary: Umar bin Khattaab urges people to weigh themselves before they are weighed, and Anas reports Umar's fear of Allaah while alone in an orchard.
notes: Two separate reports: Thaabit bin Hajjaaj's report of Umar's words, then Anas's report of Umar in the orchard.

summary: Jaabir bin Samurah tells Simaak that the Prophet was a man who often remained silent.
Abu Maalik Ashja'ee reports that his father said the Companions never saw anyone as silent as the Prophet, who only smiled when others talked too much.
notes: The father, who speaks the words, is not named and is left out. Abu Maalik Ashja'ee is not the same person as Abu Maalik Ash'ari in the list.

summary: Ubaadah bin Saamit reports that Mu'aadh bin Jabal asked what deeds to do after the Prophet, and the Prophet taught that remaining silent except for good speech is the greatest restraint on the self.
notes: Cut off mid-sentence at 'you will be (1)'; the rest of the narration is not in this chunk.

summary: Abu Hurayrah reports the Prophet telling a weeping woman not to call a slain man a martyr, and Anas reports the same about a Companion who died at Uhud.
notes: Two reports: Abu Hurayrah's, then Anas's ('In another narration'). The martyr and his mother are unnamed and left out.

summary: Khaalid bin Numayr reports that Ammaar bin Yaasir often stayed silent for long periods and seemed depressed, and when he did speak it was mostly to seek Allaah's protection from trials.
Abu Idress Khowlani recounts seeing a quiet, respected man in the Masjid of Damascus and learning from him a du'aa for steadfastness, gratitude, a pure heart and a truthful tongue.
notes: A footnote fragment in the middle of the text is OCR debris and was ignored. The unnamed man in Damascus is left out.

summary: Shaddaad relays the Prophet's du'aa for steadfastness and forgiveness, which the Prophet advised people to fill their treasures with instead of gold and silver hoarding.
notes: Identified as Shaddaad bin Aws from the context of this du'aa. The list also has Shaddaad ibnul Haad and Shaddaad bin Abdillaah, so this is an inference from the text.

summary: Isa bin Uqba reports that Abdullaah bin Mas'ood swore nothing on earth deserves a long prison sentence more than the tongue.
Abdullaah bin Mas'ood warns to beware of futile speech and to say only what will get one's needs fulfilled.
Abdullaah bin Mas'ood says those guilty of the most sins on the Day of Qiyaamah will be those who engaged most in idle talk.
Ali bin Abi Taalib gives several sayings on the tongue and silence: the tongue governs the whole body, keep a low profile, silence leads to Jannah, and a couplet on keeping secrets.
notes: Several separate sayings and couplets. The reference line to Abu Nu'aym's Hilya is editorial and is left out. Abu Dardaa is named in the heading only, not in the text.

summary: Abu Dardaa advises learning silence as one learns speech, listening more than speaking, and not speaking or laughing about things that do not concern you.
notes: The second theme is a judgement call; the saying is mainly about self-control in speech.

summary: Abu Dardaa says the tongue is the limb a believer is loved for most, since it leads him to Jannah, and the limb a disbeliever is hated for most, since it leads him to Jahannam.
Abdullaah bin Umar says a person most needs to purify his tongue, and Anas says no one attains Taqwa until he controls his tongue.
notes: Two separate sayings, from Abdullaah bin Umar and from Anas.

summary: Heading only, 'The Speech of Rasulullaah', with no narration under it.
notes: Section heading only.

summary: Aa'isha describes how clearly the Prophet spoke, so that his words could be counted, and tells how she missed a chance to rebuke a man who spoke loudly beside her room.
notes: The loud man is unnamed and left out.

summary: Aa'isha says the Prophet's speech was so clear that everyone understood it and he never spoke continuously and quickly, and a Companion said each of his letters was distinctly pronounced.
notes: The text says it was Jaabir or Abdullaah bin Umar who said the last line, and does not decide which. Jaabir is a bare name, so it is recorded without an id; it could be Jaabir bin Abdillaah or Jaabir bin Samurah.

summary: Anas reports that when the Prophet said something important he repeated it three times, and that he greeted a gathering three times.
Thumamah bin Anas reports that Anas repeated important words three times, saying the Prophet did the same so that people would understand him.
notes: Anas is the subject because the habit described is his own, and he also reports the Prophet's habit.

summary: Abu Hurayrah reports the Prophet's words that he was given concise yet comprehensive speech and the keys to the treasures of the heavens and the earth, and Abdullaah bin Salaam reports that the Prophet looked to the sky when he sat to talk.
notes: Two reports: Abu Hurayrah's, then Abdullaah bin Salaam's.

summary: Amr bin Al Aas says the Prophet gave his full attention to whoever he spoke with, and recounts asking whether he, Abu Bakr, Umar or Uthmaan was best, then regretting the questions.
notes: Uthmaan is read as Uthmaan bin Affaan, the Companion in the ranking.

summary: Aa'isha says she never saw the Prophet laugh so much that his uvula showed, and that he only smiled.
notes: OCR debris in the reporting line ('Sglgieff.says') was ignored.

summary: Abdullaah bin Haarith bin Jaz says he never saw anyone smile as much as the Prophet, and that the Prophet never laughed but only smiled.
notes: Not in the list, so no id is given.

summary: Simaak bin Harb reports asking Jaabir bin Samurah whether he was often with the Prophet, and Jaabir describes the Prophet smiling while the Companions laughed about pre-Islamic matters.

Simaak bin Harb reports that Jaabir bin Samurah described the Prophet as often silent and laughing very little, and only smiling when the Companions recited poetry and he said something that made them laugh.
Husayn bin Yazeed Kalbi says he never saw the Prophet laugh, only smile, and that at times he had to tie a rock to his belly from hunger.
notes: Not in the list. Not the same person as Dihya Kalbi.

summary: Amrah asks Aa'isha how the Prophet behaved at home, and Aa'isha replies that he was the noblest and most compassionate of men and often laughed and smiled.
Jaabir says that when revelation came or the Prophet was giving a lecture he looked like a warner, but otherwise he had the most smiling face, was the most jovial, and was the handsomest of men.
notes: Bare name 'Jaabir' with no id: it could be Jaabir bin Samurah (named in the surrounding reports) or another Jaabir. Not attributed, to avoid a wrong id.

summary: The text is garbled: Abu Umaamah's report is cut off, and Abu Dharr says he saw the Prophet smile so widely that his molars were visible.
notes: Starts mid-sentence ('Rasulullaah was one of the most quickly...'), and Abu Umaamah's report is garbled by OCR. A quoted line about other sins may belong to another report. Abu Dharr is recorded as abu-dharr-ghifaari, the list's id for that name.

summary: Abdullaah bin Mas'ood reports the Prophet's account of the last person to leave Jahannam, who is granted Jannah and ten times what the world had to offer, and says the Prophet then smiled so widely his molars showed.
Khaarijah bin Zaid says the Prophet was the most dignified person in his gatherings and never stretched his limbs out towards people while seated.
notes: Not in the list; not the same as Khaarijah bin Hudhaafah.

summary: Shahr bin Howshab and Abu Muslim Khowlaani describe how the Companions turned to Mu'aadh bin Jabal, who was quiet and dignified, for verification of hadith, and Mu'aadh identifies himself as the youthful man in the second account.
notes: Three reports: Shahr bin Howshab's, then two by Abu Muslim Khowlaani. Umar appears only as a date reference (early years of his Khilaafah).

summary: Abu Barzah says he wanted to execute a man who spoke harshly to Abu Bakr, but Abu Bakr rebuked him, and Umar says no sip is better than a sip of anger held back.
notes: Two parts: Abu Barzah's account of Abu Bakr, then a separate saying of Umar. The man who spoke harshly is unnamed and left out.

summary: Ubay bin Ka'b says he would have killed a man seen visiting his father's wife, and the Prophet laughs and says he is more possessive than Ubay, and Allaah is more possessive than the Prophet.
notes: The man who reported the matter is unnamed and left out.

summary: Mughierah reports that Sa'd bin Ubaadah said he would strike any man found with his wife, and the Prophet replied that he and Allaah are more possessive; Abu Hurayrah and Ibn Abbaas add the four-witness ruling and the Companions' plea for Sa'd.
notes: Three reports: Mughierah's, Abu Hurayrah's, and Ibn Abbaas's. Mughierah is recorded as mughiera-bin-shuba, the usual narrator of this hadith, but the text gives only the name, so this is an inference. The Companions in Ibn Abbaas's report are unnamed.

summary: Aa'isha tells of her jealousy of Umm Salama, which she and Hafsah discussed, then the Qur'an verse on monasticism, and Mu'aadh bin Jabal's warning against forsaking enjoining good.
notes: Several reports: Aa'isha's account, the monasticism passage with its verse, another narration about those who were martyred, and Mu'aadh bin Jabal's report. The text ends mid-sentence ('The Rank on the Day of Qiyaamah of those who'); the next item, n02078, is headed 'enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil' and may be the rest.

summary: Yazeed Raqaashi reports from Anas that the Prophet described people who travel to advise others, and who become beloved to Allaah by making His servants beloved to Him through enjoining good and forbidding evil.
notes: Anas asks the question, so he is recorded as subject.

summary: Hudhayfah asks the Prophet when people will abandon enjoining good and forbidding evil, and the Prophet answers that it will be when the affliction of the Bani Israa'eel befalls them: leniency towards sinners, knowledge given to the worst, and leadership to the young.
notes: The text says only 'Hudhayfah'. Recorded as Hudhayfah bin Yamaan, the best-known Companion of that name; the list also has Hudhayfah bin Mihsin. OCR renders 'Israa'eel' as 'lsraa'eel'.

summary: Qais bin Abu Haazim reports that when Abu Bakr became Khalifah he warned people against misreading the verse about looking after oneself, citing the Prophet's words that punishment reaches all when evil is seen and not changed.
notes: The list has two near-identical entries for this name (qais-bin-abi-haazim and qais-bin-abu-haazim); qais-bin-abu-haazim is used.
